title: Mi, tu, su: possessives
why: After the units on the present tense and getting around town, this lesson opens the unit on the people around us: possessives and family vocabulary. It sorts out the traps for English speakers (mis with a plural noun, su for his, her, their and the polite your, nuestra for a feminine noun) and gets you ready to describe people and talk about likes in the next lessons.

Mi, tu, su: whose is it?

Good news first: mi, tu and su don't change for gender, just like English “my,” “your,” “his.” You say mi padre and mi madre. The difference is that the Spanish possessive agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner, so it takes an -s when the thing is plural: mis libros, my books. English “my” never changes; Spanish “my” does.

OwnerOne thingSeveral thingsEnglish
yomimismy
tútutusyour
él, ella, ustedsusushis, her, its, your (polite)
nosotros, nosotrasnuestro, nuestranuestros, nuestrasour
vosotros, vosotrasvuestro, vuestravuestros, vuestrasyour (plural)
ellos, ellas, ustedessusustheir, your (plural, polite)

Nuestro and vuestro: four forms

Only nuestro and vuestro also agree in gender, like an -o / -a adjective: nuestro piso, nuestra casa, nuestros hijos, nuestras amigas. The gender is the gender of the thing, never of the owner: two men say nuestra casa, because casa is feminine.

Vivimos en Toledo con nuestras hijas.We live in Toledo with our daughters.

Never an article in front

Just like in English, there's no article before the possessive: mi casa, never “la mi casa.” If you're also learning Italian, careful: la mia casa doesn't translate word for word.

Don't mix up tu (your) and tú (you, the subject): Tú vives con tu hermano. The possessive never has an accent.

", "

Su: one word, several owners

Su and sus do the work of “his,” “her,” “its,” “their” and the polite “your,” all on their own. That's handy, but sometimes ambiguous: su coche can be Pablo's car, Lucía's, my neighbors'… or yours.

SpanishEnglish
Pablo vive con su madre.Pablo lives with his mother.
Lucía habla con sus primos.Lucía is talking with her cousins.
Mis vecinos venden su piso.My neighbors are selling their apartment.
Señora López, ¿cómo se llama su hijo?Mrs. López, what's your son's name?

Context almost always makes it clear. If there's any doubt, you clarify with de + the person, after the noun: el coche de él (his car), la casa de ella (her house), la maleta de usted (your suitcase).

¿Es el móvil de Diego o el móvil de Marta? — Es el móvil de ella.Is it Diego's phone or Marta's phone? — It's hers.

Mío, tuyo: “mine,” “yours”

In answer to ¿De quién es? (Whose is it?), you'll hear long forms. For now, just learn to recognize them: Es mío (it's mine), Es tuyo (it's yours), Es suyo (it's his, it's hers). Unlike English “mine,” they agree with the object: la maleta → es mía, las llaves → son tuyas.

¿De quién es la chaqueta? — Es mía.Whose jacket is this? — It's mine.

For now, just say Es mi chaqueta: it's correct and natural. Mío and tuyo will come back later.

", "

La familia

Almost all family words come in -o / -a pairs. The masculine plural also covers a mixed group: mis hermanos means “my brothers,” but also “my brothers and sisters,” my siblings.

SpanishEnglishPluralEnglish
el padre / la madrefather / motherlos padresparents
el hermano / la hermanabrother / sisterlos hermanossiblings, brothers and sisters
el hijo / la hijason / daughterlos hijoschildren (sons and daughters)
el abuelo / la abuelagrandfather / grandmotherlos abuelosgrandparents
el nieto / la nietagrandson / granddaughterlos nietosgrandchildren
el tío / la tíauncle / auntlos tíosaunts and uncles
el primo / la primacousin (male / female)los primoscousins
el sobrino / la sobrinanephew / niecelos sobrinosnieces and nephews
el suegro / la suegrafather-in-law / mother-in-lawlos suegrosin-laws (parents-in-law)

For couples: el marido (husband), la mujer (wife, and also “woman”) and la pareja, very common, which means “partner” whatever the gender, and also “couple.”

Tengo dos hermanos: un hermano mayor y una hermana pequeña.I have two siblings: an older brother and a younger sister.
Mis padres viven en Zaragoza y mis abuelos viven con ellos.My parents live in Zaragoza and my grandparents live with them.

False friend: your parents are los padres (father and mother). The word los parientes exists, but it means relatives, the extended family, not “parents.” And a family's “children” are los hijos: ¿Tienes hijos? (Do you have kids?)
